# Results {#sec-results .deo-results}

## Overview of cases

The eight included cases span 2014 to the present and come from Europe,
Indonesia, the United States and an international patient network (@tbl-case-overview).
Four are mental-health citizen science projects, two are Indonesian citizen
health-data initiatives that arose during the COVID-19 pandemic, and two are
failures involving data from people in mental distress. Leading roles were held
by citizens who founded the initiative in two cases (LaporCovid-19 and the
Patient-Led Research Collaborative), shared between a university and
lived-experience co-researchers in one (CoAct), and held by institutions in the
remaining five. Evidence was strongest for the Patient-Led Research
Collaborative and LaporCovid-19, each documented in peer-reviewed articles, and
weakest for Youth-GEMS, which has not yet published results, and Samaritans
Radar, which is documented in grey literature and news.

## Case narratives

### CoAct for Mental Health

CoAct for Mental Health was part of a European citizen social science project
funded under Horizon 2020. In 2020, an open call recruited people with lived
experience of mental health problems and family members as co-researchers,
recognised as experts in the field [@casanovas2026]. The research focused on
social support networks, a need identified by the communities themselves.
Co-researchers took part in formulating the research questions, co-designed a
chatbot on the messaging app Telegram, and wrote the micro-stories of social
support that the chatbot shared with participants. The chatbot reached up to
900 people; the analysed dataset contained 11,002 interactions from 394
participants responding to 129 stories. Analysis was carried out by the
research group and interpreted collectively with the co-researchers and a wider
coalition that included representatives of the mental health system. In
November 2022, a community assembly approved 14 recommendations, which were
presented to Barcelona City Council and to the regional mental health pact, and
published as policy briefs [@casanovas2026]. We found no documentation of
whether these recommendations were adopted. The chatbot allowed anonymous
participation on a sensitive topic, and the authors note the need for emotional
safety. The project won the 2024 European Union Prize for Citizen Science.

*Lesson:* shared governance with people with lived experience produces co-owned
questions and policy proposals, but whether those proposals are used depends on
commitments from decision-makers secured before the project ends.

### HoeGekIsNL

HoeGekIsNL ("How crazy is the Netherlands?"; published in English as
HowNutsAreTheDutch) is a national crowdsourcing study initiated by an academic
research centre in Groningen to map the mental strengths and vulnerabilities of
the Dutch population [@vanderkrieke2016; @mindwise2016]. Members of the public
enrolled themselves through a website and completed questionnaires on both
psychiatric symptoms and mental strengths and resources; a subgroup also
reported on their smartphones three times a day for 30 days. In total, 12,503
people took part [@vanderkrieke2016]. Participants were not paid. Instead, they
received personalised feedback and could compare themselves with other
participants; those who completed most of the diary received an automatically
generated report on patterns in their emotions and behaviour, and on how their
strengths and vulnerabilities interacted [@mindwise2016]. We found no
documentation of public involvement in choosing the questions or designing the
study. Although participation was intended for adults, the study team reported
that more than 200 minors took part [@mindwise2016], which illustrates a
safeguarding challenge of open online enrolment. At the time of writing, the
study website still invited new participants and also offered a COVID-19
questionnaire [@hoegekis_web].

*Lesson:* personal feedback can be both the incentive that brings people in at
scale and the means of returning results to them. Measuring strengths alongside
symptoms is feasible at population scale.

### Patient-Led Research Collaborative

The Patient-Led Research Collaborative was formed in May 2020 by people with
Long COVID who met in an online support group [@mccorkell2021]. Patients
designed a survey, drawing on their own and their communities' experience to
compile the list of symptoms, translated it into eight languages, and analysed
responses from 3,762 people [@davis2020preprint; @davis2021]. Fatigue,
post-exertional malaise (worsening after effort) and cognitive dysfunction were
the most common symptoms, reported by 98.3%, 89.0% and 85.1% of respondents,
respectively. The study had ethics approval and the authors reported its main
limitation, a sample drawn from active support-group members. The collaborative
published the first report on Long COVID [@fitzgerald2024], and its members,
all patients, were the authors. In 2022, a panel of 15 patient-researchers
allocated USD 4.8 million in research grants to ten projects [@plrc_fund]. We
found no documentation of whether survey respondents received results directly,
or of public access to the dataset.

*Lesson:* when people who live with a condition lead the research, questions
that conventional research has not yet asked come to light quickly. Credibility
came from rigorous methods and peer-reviewed publication, not from patient
status alone.

### Youth-GEMS

Youth-GEMS is a five-year project funded by Horizon Europe with 18 partners in
ten countries, studying how genetic and environmental factors shape mental
health in people aged 12 to 24 [@prbb2023]. Its research questions and design
were set by the consortium. Young Experts, aged 18 to 25 with lived experience
of mental health problems, are recruited with a partner youth organisation
[@youthgems_expert2025]. They shaped the wording, tone and visuals of the
project's mobile app and identified problems that technical teams had not
considered, but they were explicitly not involved in building or validating the
artificial-intelligence model, which remained with technical experts and
psychiatrists [@youthgems_decisions2025]. A framework for regular involvement,
data protection and safe spaces for sharing experience was established, and
young people's feedback is used to assess the quality of engagement
[@youthgems_earma2024]. Young Experts receive training and vouchers rather than
pay [@youthgems_expert2025]. A clinical study of about 1,000 young people in
Europe and 1,000 in Australia was under way at the time of writing, and no
results had been published [@youthgems_research].

*Lesson:* institution-led projects tend to limit citizen roles to consultation
on selected components. Stating openly where involvement stops, and why, is
more credible than implying full partnership.

### LaporCovid-19

LaporCovid-19 was founded in March 2020 by a coalition of public health
experts, scientists, journalists and activists in response to the lack of
reliable COVID-19 data in Indonesia [@laporcovid2021; @rinaldi2024]. Citizens
reported cases, deaths, and experiences through a chatbot on WhatsApp and
Telegram. From September 2020, about 35 volunteers maintained a database of
health-worker deaths, searching obituaries in online news and social media and
collecting testimonies from families and colleagues [@ekawati2022]. Using these
data, an analysis with ethics approval from the Ministry of Health's research
ethics committee documented 1,545 health-worker deaths and estimated that
health workers died at 4.92 times the rate of the general population, at a time
when no official count of health-worker infections or deaths existed
[@ekawati2022]. Aggregated data were made publicly available. The group
advocated for compensation for families of health workers, and civil-society
pressure contributed to the withdrawal of a self-funded vaccination plan
[@laporcovid2021]. Its relationship with government was contested, as its data
directly challenged official figures [@laporcovid2021]. We found no
documentation of the project's current status or of measures to protect
volunteers.

*Lesson:* citizen data can document what official statistics leave out. A
critical stance toward government protects independence but may limit uptake.

### Community-based surveillance by the Indonesian Red Cross

The Indonesian Red Cross (*Palang Merah Indonesia*) ran community-based
surveillance in eight villages across four districts, including Boyolali in
Central Java, as part of an international epidemic preparedness programme
[@ifrc2021]. The system was designed by the Red Cross with community and
government stakeholders. Volunteers recruited from local structures, such as
community leaders, midwives and teachers, were trained to recognise and report
signs of priority diseases. Between September 2019 and September 2020, they
raised 55 alerts, of which 48 were verified as true, and every alert received a
response within 24 hours. Alerts were fed into the national early-warning
system, and local governments took ownership; Boyolali prioritised the
programme in its local budget [@ifrc2021]. Data were protected by recording
only initials and sending numeric codes by text message. Volunteers reported to
a protocol designed by others and had no role in analysis. Volunteers were
unpaid, which the report identifies as a challenge for retention. Of 234
volunteers trained in surveillance, 171 (73%) remained active.

*Lesson:* building citizen reporting into existing government systems makes it
last, at the cost of keeping citizens at the reporting stage. Volunteer
retention needs planning and resources.

### Crisis Text Line data sharing

Crisis Text Line is a free text-message crisis service in the United States,
staffed by trained volunteer counsellors. It ran a programme sharing anonymised
conversation data with academic researchers under published guidelines for
non-commercial use. It also created a for-profit subsidiary, Loris.ai, which
was licensed Crisis Text Line data to train customer-service software
[@eysenbach2025]. People texting in crisis had agreed only to a
terms-of-service link. After the arrangement was reported in the press in
January 2022 and a commissioner of the US Federal Communications Commission
called for it to stop, Crisis Text Line ended the relationship within three
days and asked Loris.ai to delete the data. A former volunteer had raised
concerns about consent and conflict of interest, and the journal that had
published the original data-sharing guidelines issued a correction clarifying
the authors' ties to the commercial and non-commercial entities
[@eysenbach2025]. Texters had no role in the research beyond being its data
subjects.

*Lesson:* consent given in a moment of crisis, through a terms-of-service link,
does not cover a later commercial use. A change of purpose requires new consent
and new ethical review, and ties to commercial beneficiaries must be disclosed.

### Samaritans Radar

Samaritans Radar was an app launched by the UK suicide-prevention charity
Samaritans on 29 October 2014 [@responsibledata_radar]. Based on university
research, it scanned the tweets of accounts that an app user followed for
language associated with suicidal intent and emailed the user an alert with
suggested actions. The people whose tweets were scanned were not told.
Monitoring was on by default; people could ask to be excluded only if they knew
the app existed. Many in the UK mental health community objected that tweets
which were technically public were not expected to be monitored, that people
might stop sharing, and that stalkers or bullies could use the alerts to find
people at their most vulnerable [@responsibledata_radar]. Samaritans suspended
the app nine days after launch [@irishtimes2014] and closed it permanently in
March 2015, deleting all associated data. The charity stated that it should
have consulted more widely, and it later ran a public consultation on digital
tools [@responsibledata_radar].

*Lesson:* a post being technically public does not mean its author has agreed
to be monitored. Tools that use mental-health data should be designed with the
people being watched, not only the people watching, and should require opt-in.
